Stratified Designs

Gosuke Homma

2026-10-24

Source: vignettes/bbssr-stratified.Rmd
bbssr-stratified.Rmd
library(bbssr)

Design and notation

A trial is stratified into J≥2J \ge 2 strata, for example by centre or by a baseline factor, and stratum jj has N1jN_{1j} patients in group 1 and N2jN_{2j} in group 2, both fixed by the design. Let x1jx_{1j} and x2jx_{2j} be the numbers of responders of the two groups and zj=x1j+x2jz_j = x_{1j} + x_{2j} the number of responders of the stratum. All tests of the Strat* functions use S=∑jx1jS = \sum_j x_{1j}, the number of responders of group 1 summed over the strata. Given z=(z1,…,zJ)z = (z_1, \ldots, z_J), the null expectation of SS is E=∑jN1jzj/NjE = \sum_j N_{1j} z_j / N_j with Nj=N1j+N2jN_j = N_{1j} + N_{2j}, and each test rejects when SS is at most a lower or at least an upper critical value.

The functions follow those for two independent groups: StratRR(), StratPower() and StratSampleSize() for the fixed design, and StratPowerBSSR(), StratBSSR(), StratTypeIErrorBSSR() and StratAlphaAdjBSSR() for blinded sample size re-estimation.

Tests

Five stratified tests are available. 'CMH' is the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel statistic (S−E)/V(S - E) / \sqrt{V} with the hypergeometric variance V=∑jN1jN2jzj(Nj−zj)/{Nj2(Nj−1)}V = \sum_j N_{1j} N_{2j} z_j (N_j - z_j) / \{N_j^2 (N_j - 1)\}, and 'Cochran' is Cochran’s statistic with the binomial variance ∑jN1jN2jzj(Nj−zj)/Nj3\sum_j N_{1j} N_{2j} z_j (N_j - z_j) / N_j^3, the statistic of Woolson et al. (1986). 'CMH-cc' and 'Cochran-cc' reduce |S−E||S - E| by 0.5 when it is at least 0.5, the continuity correction of stats::mantelhaen.test(). Nam (1992) reduces S−ES - E by 0.5 in every outcome; the two corrections reject the same outcomes at one-sided levels up to 0.078, since an outcome with |S−E|<0.5|S - E| < 0.5 has a larger one-sided p-value. 'Strat-Fisher' is the stratified exact conditional test of Jung (2014), which refers SS to its distribution given zz, the convolution of the hypergeometric distributions of the strata. Three unstratified tests, which analyse the table of totals and ignore the strata, are available for comparison (see Analyses that ignore the strata).

Jung (2014, Table 2) analyses the response to thymosin in three strata of patients with bronchogenic carcinoma.

thymosin <- array(c(10, 12, 1, 1, 9, 11, 0, 1, 8, 7, 0, 3), c(2, 2, 3))
p.exact <- stats::mantelhaen.test(thymosin, alternative = 'greater', exact = TRUE)$p.value
p.mh <- stats::mantelhaen.test(thymosin, alternative = 'greater', correct = FALSE)$p.value
round(c(exact = p.exact, mh = p.mh), 4)
#>  exact     mh 
#> 0.1563 0.0760

The one-sided p-values 0.1563 and 0.0760 are those of Jung (2014) for the stratified exact test and the Mantel-Haenszel test, which 'Strat-Fisher' and 'CMH' compute in the same way. StratRR() lists the critical values of a design for every vector of stratum totals.

rr <- StratRR(N1 = c(10, 12), N2 = c(10, 12), alpha = 0.025, Test = 'Strat-Fisher')
print(rr, n = 6)
#> Rejection region of a stratified test
#> 
#>   Test             : Strat-Fisher
#>   Alternative      : greater
#>   Group sizes      : N1 = (10, 12), N2 = (10, 12)
#>   Alpha            : 0.025
#>   Combinations     : 525, of which 457 have a rejected value of S
#> 
#>  z.S1 z.S2 S.min S.max lower upper
#>     5    0     0     5    NA     5
#>     6    0     0     6    NA     6
#>     7    0     0     7    NA     7
#>     8    0     0     8    NA     7
#>     9    0     0     9    NA     8
#>    10    0     0    10    NA     8
#>   ... 451 more rows

Power and sample size

The power is the probability of the rejection region when the numbers of responders are binomial in every group and stratum. It is computed exactly for any number of strata and any response probabilities, so the odds ratio need not be common to the strata. The normal approximation to the total sample size is formula (2.8) of Woolson et al. (1986), and with a continuity correction formula (2.3) of Nam (1992). A design is described by the fractions of the strata and the allocation ratio, and the exact search runs over the total sample size within this family.

p2 <- c(0.3, 0.5)
p1 <- p2 * 2.5 / (1 - p2 + p2 * 2.5)
ss.std <- StratSampleSize(p1, p2, frac = c(0.4, 0.6), alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8,
                          Test = 'CMH', method = 'standard')
ss.cmh <- StratSampleSize(p1, p2, frac = c(0.4, 0.6), alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8,
                          Test = 'CMH')
ss.exact <- StratSampleSize(p1, p2, frac = c(0.4, 0.6), alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8,
                            Test = 'Strat-Fisher')
c(standard = ss.std$N, CMH = ss.cmh$N, exact = ss.exact$N)
#> standard      CMH    exact 
#>      160      164      176

With a common odds ratio of 2.5, the normal approximation gives a total of 160 patients, at which the exact power of the CMH test is 0.796. The exact search gives 164 patients for the CMH test and 176 for the stratified exact test, whose conditional control of the type I error rate makes it conservative.

Blinded sample size re-estimation

At an interim analysis the numbers of responders of every stratum can be counted without unblinding. The blinded estimate of the pooled response probability of stratum jj is sjs_j divided by the interim size of the stratum. It is divided between the groups with the assumed effect Delta.A, common to the strata on the scale effect, and the total sample size is re-estimated for these probabilities and divided between the strata as in the planned design. With two strata the final sizes depend on the interim data only through (s1,s2)(s_1, s_2), and the power is computed exactly by enumeration. With a common odds ratio the planning probabilities of a stratum whose pooled estimate is close to 0 or 1 are close to each other, so the examples bound the final total by twice the planned total with N.max.

plan <- StratSampleSize(p1, p2, frac = c(0.5, 0.5), alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8,
                        Test = 'CMH', method = 'standard')
pooled <- (p1 + p2) / 2
res <- StratPowerBSSR(p = rbind(pooled, pooled + 0.1), Delta.A = 2.5, Delta.T = 2.5,
                      N1 = plan$N1, N2 = plan$N2, omega = 0.5, r = 1, alpha = 0.025,
                      tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'CMH', effect = 'OR',
                      ss.method = 'standard', N.max = 2 * plan$N)
res
#> Blinded sample size re-estimation for a stratified design
#> 
#>   Test             : CMH
#>   Alternative      : greater
#>   Re-estimation    : normal approximation (unrestricted)
#>   Planned sizes    : (40, 40) and (40, 40)
#>   Interim sizes    : (20, 20) and (20, 20)
#>   Effect           : OR, assumed 2.5, true 2.5
#>   Alpha            : 0.025, target power 0.8
#> 
#>       p.S1      p.S2     p1.S1     p1.S2     p2.S1     p2.S2 power.BSSR
#>  0.4086207 0.6071429 0.5172414 0.7142857 0.3000000 0.5000000     0.8122
#>  0.5086207 0.7071429 0.6211596 0.7995566 0.3960818 0.6147291     0.8145
#>  power.TRAD    E.N
#>      0.7963 166.43
#>      0.7821 175.75

When the pooled response probabilities are those of the planning (the first row), the power of the re-estimation design is 0.812 with an expected total of 166.4. When they are 0.1 higher in both strata, the re-estimation adjusts the sample size and the power is 0.814, while that of the fixed design is 0.782.

Type I error rate

Under the null hypothesis both groups of stratum jj respond with the probability θj\theta_j. Given the interim and the second-stage numbers of responders of a stratum, the numbers of responders of group 1 are hypergeometric whatever θj\theta_j, so with two strata the type I error rate is a polynomial in (θ1,θ2)(\theta_1, \theta_2). StratTypeIErrorBSSR() computes its coefficients in the products of the Bernstein bases of the two strata, evaluates it on a grid, and certifies its largest value over the rectangle spanned by the grid: the rectangle is subdivided until the largest coefficient of every piece exceeds the largest value found by at most 10−1210^{-12}.

tie <- StratTypeIErrorBSSR(Delta.A = 2.5, N1 = c(20, 20), N2 = c(20, 20), omega = 0.5,
                           r = 1, alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'CMH',
                           effect = 'OR', ss.method = 'standard', N.max = 160,
                           theta = seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05))
tie
#> Type I error rate of blinded sample size re-estimation for a stratified design
#> 
#>   Test             : CMH
#>   Alternative      : greater
#>   Planned sizes    : (20, 20) and (20, 20)
#>   Points           : 361
#>   Maximum          : certified over (theta.S1, theta.S2) in [0.05, 0.95] x [0.05, 0.95]
#>   Alpha            : 0.025
#> 
#>        Design  theta.S1  theta.S2       TIE     bound
#>          BSSR 0.3401352 0.3401352 0.0255490 0.0255490
#>  Fixed sample 0.5000000 0.5000000 0.0283368 0.0283368
mx <- attr(tie, 'max')

The largest type I error rate of the re-estimation design with 20 patients per group and stratum is 0.02555, at (θ1,θ2)=(\theta_1, \theta_2) = (0.340, 0.340), and no rate in the rectangle exceeds 0.02555. That of the fixed design is 0.02834.

plot(tie)

StratAlphaAdjBSSR() lowers the nominal level until the certified largest rate does not exceed alpha.

adj <- StratAlphaAdjBSSR(Delta.A = 2.5, N1 = c(20, 20), N2 = c(20, 20), omega = 0.5,
                         r = 1, alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'CMH',
                         effect = 'OR', ss.method = 'standard', N.max = 160,
                         theta = seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05))
adj
#> Adjusted significance level for blinded sample size re-estimation
#> 
#>   Test            : CMH
#>   Alternative     : greater
#>   Adjusted part   : final analysis only
#>   Maximum         : certified over (theta.S1, theta.S2) in [0.05, 0.95] x [0.05, 0.95]
#>   Target level    : 0.025
#> 
#>        Design   max.TIE alpha.adj max.TIE.adj
#>          BSSR 0.0255490 0.0245872   0.0248681
#>  Fixed sample 0.0283368 0.0228356   0.0246744

StratCondRejectBSSR() gives, under the null hypothesis, the probability of rejection given the pooled numbers of responders of the strata at the interim analysis and in the second stage. These probabilities do not depend on (θ1,θ2)(\theta_1, \theta_2), and averaging them over the second stage gives the type I error rate given the interim outcome. Below they are evaluated at the point of the largest rate found above.

crp <- StratCondRejectBSSR(Delta.A = 2.5, N1 = c(20, 20), N2 = c(20, 20), omega = 0.5,
                           r = 1, alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'CMH',
                           effect = 'OR', ss.method = 'standard', N.max = 160,
                           theta = cbind(mx$theta.S1[1], mx$theta.S2[1]))
#> Warning in data.frame(theta.S1 = pts[p, 1], theta.S2 = pts[p, 2], s1 = map$s1,
#> : row names were found from a short variable and have been discarded
crp
#> Conditional rejection probabilities of blinded sample size re-estimation
#> for a stratified design, under equal response probabilities in every stratum
#> 
#>   Test             : CMH
#>   Alternative      : greater
#>   Planned sizes    : (20, 20) and (20, 20)
#>   Interim sizes    : (10, 10) and (10, 10)
#>   Assumed effect   : 2.5 (OR)
#>   Nominal level    : 0.025
#>   Interim outcomes : 441 pairs (s1, s2)
#>   Above the level  : 267496 outcomes for CRP, 762792 for CRP.total
#> 
#> Largest conditional rejection probability
#>   Quantity   value s1 s2 w1 w2
#>        CRP 0.06250  1  1  1  1
#>  CRP.total 0.06093  1  0  1  2
#> 
#> Type I error rate over 1 point: largest 0.02555 at theta = (0.340135, 0.340135)
by.s <- attr(crp, 'by.s')
head(by.s[order(-by.s$contribution), ], 5)
#>      theta.S1  theta.S2 s1 s2     prob.s      TIE.s contribution
#> 155 0.3401352 0.3401352  7  7 0.03371154 0.02640780 0.0008902478
#> 134 0.3401352 0.3401352  7  6 0.03270032 0.02633070 0.0008610225
#> 154 0.3401352 0.3401352  6  7 0.03270032 0.02633070 0.0008610225
#> 133 0.3401352 0.3401352  6  6 0.03171943 0.02617832 0.0008303614
#> 176 0.3401352 0.3401352  7  8 0.02823765 0.02625803 0.0007414652

The contributions of the interim outcomes sum to 0.02555, the largest type I error rate found above.

Analyses that ignore the strata

'Unstrat-Chisq' is Pearson’s chi-squared test of the table of totals, with ∑jN1j\sum_j N_{1j} and ∑jN2j\sum_j N_{2j} patients and ∑jzj\sum_j z_j responders, which is the comparison of two proportions with the pooled variance; 'Unstrat-Chisq-cc' adds the continuity correction, and 'Unstrat-Fisher' is Fisher’s exact test of that table. Their critical values depend on zz only through ∑jzj\sum_j z_j, but their power and type I error rate are computed with the response probabilities of each stratum. An unstratified test controls the level when the strata are distributed alike in the two groups, and its level can be distorted otherwise (Nam, 1992; Jung, 2014). In the next design group 1 holds a third of the first stratum, whose patients respond rarely, and three quarters of the second.

th <- rbind(c(0.2, 0.6), c(0.4, 0.4))
lev <- sapply(c('CMH', 'Strat-Fisher', 'Unstrat-Chisq', 'Unstrat-Fisher'), function(Test) {
  StratPower(th, th, N1 = c(20, 60), N2 = c(40, 20), alpha = 0.025, Test = Test)$Power
})
rownames(lev) <- c('theta = (0.2, 0.6)', 'theta = (0.4, 0.4)')
round(lev, 4)
#>                       CMH Strat-Fisher Unstrat-Chisq Unstrat-Fisher
#> theta = (0.2, 0.6) 0.0264       0.0157        0.5090         0.4348
#> theta = (0.4, 0.4) 0.0247       0.0160        0.0247         0.0166

With the response probabilities 0.2 and 0.6 in the two strata, the one-sided type I error rate of the unstratified chi-squared test is 0.509 instead of 0.025, because the table of totals compares groups made of different mixtures of the strata. When the strata respond alike, the rate is 0.0247.

The re-estimation can ignore the strata as well: with ss.strata = 'pooled' the sample size is re-estimated from the proportion of responders among all the interim patients, used for every stratum, so the final sizes depend only on the total number of interim responders. The final analysis is still the test given by Test.

res.pooled <- StratPowerBSSR(p = rbind(pooled, pooled + 0.1), Delta.A = 2.5,
                             Delta.T = 2.5, N1 = plan$N1, N2 = plan$N2, omega = 0.5, r = 1,
                             alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'CMH', effect = 'OR',
                             ss.method = 'standard', N.max = 2 * plan$N,
                             ss.strata = 'pooled')
rbind(stratified = res$E.N, pooled = res.pooled$E.N)
#>                [,1]     [,2]
#> stratified 166.4284 175.7539
#> pooled     157.1181 165.4599

The rows give the expected final totals of the two estimates in the two scenarios of the previous section.

Three or more strata

With three or more strata the number of interim outcomes grows as a product over the strata, and StratPowerBSSR() and StratTypeIErrorBSSR() estimate the rates of the re-estimation design by simulation, with the random numbers of R and a Monte Carlo standard error. The rates of the fixed design remain exact.

set.seed(1)
q2 <- c(0.2, 0.35, 0.5)
q1 <- q2 * 2.5 / (1 - q2 + q2 * 2.5)
plan3 <- StratSampleSize(q1, q2, frac = c(0.3, 0.3, 0.4), alpha = 0.025,
                         tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'CMH', method = 'standard')
res3 <- StratPowerBSSR(p = (q1 + q2) / 2, Delta.A = 2.5, Delta.T = 2.5, N1 = plan3$N1,
                       N2 = plan3$N2, omega = 0.5, r = 1, alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8,
                       Test = 'CMH', effect = 'OR', ss.method = 'standard',
                       N.max = 2 * plan3$N, nsim = 2e4)
res3[, c('power.BSSR', 'se.BSSR', 'power.TRAD', 'E.N')]
#>   power.BSSR     se.BSSR power.TRAD      E.N
#> 1    0.82235 0.002702688  0.8033501 175.9536

References

Jung SH (2014). Stratified Fisher’s exact test and its sample size calculation. Biometrical Journal, 56(1), 129-140.

Nam J (1992). Sample size determination for case-control studies and the comparison of stratified and unstratified analyses. Biometrics, 48(2), 389-395.

Woolson RF, Bean JA, Rojas PB (1986). Sample size for case-control studies using Cochran’s statistic. Biometrics, 42(4), 927-932.
